chunks.text:
Hi Simone,

I watched you grow into a different person this year. Actually, that's imprecise: you became more yourself, which is different from becoming different.

Q1: you were freaking out about debts, visa uncertainty, relationship strain with James, the whole question of whether California was even possible anymore. I remember crashing at your place trying to calm your nerves down, both of us on the couch running through scenarios that mostly ended badly. Q4: you were running around your childhood home taking pictures at the Christmas party, occasional hugs from James, fit and healthy and settled into a life that works. The gap between those two versions of you is the whole year.

Iris Murdoch writes about "a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality": attention directed at another person without the distortions of your own ego getting in the way.[^murdoch] I think watching you this year taught me something about that. To see you clearly, I had to stop projecting my own anxieties about what was possible onto your situation. You kept proving the projections wrong anyway.

```quotes
The love which brings the right answer is an exercise of justice and realism and really looking. The difficulty is to keep the attention fixed upon the real situation and to prevent it from returning surreptitiously to the self with consolations of self-pity, resentment, fantasy and despair.

Iris Murdoch, _The Sovereignty of Good_
```

---

Q2 was pure agency. The debts got handled (well mostly, ig). The visa situation resolved. California happened. Looking back, each step seems almost inevitable, but I was there for the uncertainty, the moments when it looked like the whole thing might collapse. What I saw was someone who kept finding the next concrete step when the path ahead was opaque.

You kept beginning. Debt didn't compute to California; relationship strain didn't compute to California; visa uncertainty didn't compute to California. And yet: California.

---

The summer picnic in Toronto was the first time I saw you settled into the new life. You'd made it through the chaos and arrived somewhere real. There's a quality Joe Carlsmith calls "green": being "importantly alive," with a kind of presence and dignity.[^carlsmith] Some people radiate this. They seem to have more reality than others, more weight in the room. At the picnic, sitting in the grass, watching you laugh about something I can't remember, I thought: she's green now. Whatever was constricted before had opened up.

---

Christmas dinner and the delinquent night before: my heart is full. You looked healthy in a way that went beyond the physical, a person who'd walked through a hard year and come out the other side more solid.

The particular joy of this year was watching the gap close between who you are and who you were becoming. What I witnessed was someone in motion. The motion looked like stress and uncertainty in Q1, like relentless problem-solving in Q2, like ease and presence in Q3 and Q4. But it was all the same motion.

---

I love you. I'm proud of you. The future you're building in California: I have no projections about it, no anxieties to offer. You've proven that you can make things work. Whatever comes next, I'll be paying attention.

More dinners. More delinquent nights. You're one of the people who makes my world bigger by being in it.

See you soon.

[^sign]

[^murdoch]: iris murdoch, _the sovereignty of good_ (1970), three essays; "the just and loving gaze" is from "the idea of perfection," and the title essay was her leslie stephen lecture of 1967. murdoch argues that moral perception IS the work: the challenge is learning to see what's actually there, without the distortions of ego. "unselfing" is the discipline of expanding awareness beyond yourself so you can come into contact with reality.

[^carlsmith]: joe carlsmith, "on green" (2024). of an old redwood: "they do, indeed, seem to have a kind of presence and dignity; they seem importantly alive."
